**Concert Pitch**

The call came on a Tuesday, the way most calls do — unremarkable, unhurried, a woman's voice asking if he still tuned pianos.

"I do," Arthur said.

"It was my mother's. She passed in March, and the house goes on the market next month. We don't know what to do with the piano. Could you look at it? Tell us honestly if it's worth saving."

He was seventy-nine. His hands had begun to file their own reports — a tremor in the mornings, a stiffness that took an hour to argue out of them. He had declared the last piano the last piano at least four times, and meant it each time.

"Saturday morning," he heard himself say. "I'll be there."

The house on Delmore Street was a two-story clapboard with the windows dark and the rooms going hollow around stacked boxes. The daughter — Carol, she said, shaking his hand like a business meeting — apologized for the mess. The piano stood against the front wall of the living room where the furniture used to be: a Baldwin upright, 1961 by the serial number, walnut veneer gone dull under a film of dust, but sound. Nobody had put a drink on it. Nobody had let the sun cook it. Somebody had loved it once, in the ordinary way people love things — by not quite neglecting them.

He raised the lid. The smell came up out of it: felt and old wood, a faint sweetness like a coat closet, dust with decades in it. He pressed the keys one at a time, ear tilted, and the piano told him its whole history in about ninety seconds. A quarter-tone flat overall — strings give up their tension by degrees across the years, the instrument sighing slowly down toward its resting pitch. The middle register worst. One dead note in the treble, a broken string. Two keys sticking. And underneath it all, a decent piano. Good bones, as the saying goes. His father had hated that saying. Pianos didn't have bones, he said. They had opinions, two hundred and thirty of them, one per string, and the tuner's job was to hold a meeting and get them to agree.

Arthur set out his tools on the bench: the tuning lever, the felt strip, the rubber wedges, the fork that hummed A-440 when you struck it — concert pitch, the note the whole world had agreed on, though nothing in physics required it. People had simply decided, together, what A should sound like. It was, his father liked to say, the only treaty that had never been broken.

He worked the way he had worked for sixty years, which was slowly. Felt strip threaded through the strings to silence the neighbors. Wedge in place. Lever on the pin, and then the listening — that slow wobble, the beat, when two tones are close enough to fight. You turn the pin a hair. A half-hair. The beat slows. Slows. Dies. On to the next. It was not, strictly speaking, work. It was attention, sustained for hours, and he had built a life out of it.

His hands, he noticed, were steady today.

The dead string he replaced from his case — the old one had rusted through at the bearing point. The sticking keys he freed, cleaned the felt, eased the bushings. And when he lifted the bench lid to make room, he found the music: lesson books, a hymnal, and on top a recital program gone soft at the folds. *Spring Recital, June 1954. Margaret Ellison, age 9 — Für Elise.* Penciled fingerings in the margins of the sheet music, in a child's careful hand, some of them wrong. He could see her: small, serious, the numbers copied out of a teacher's book, the same eight bars played four hundred times — because he could read it in the hammers too, the felt worn into grooves on exactly those notes, the left-hand figure and the melody above it, the grooves deepest where a child had practiced and a woman had returned to, off and on, for seventy years.

Carol brought him coffee around noon and watched him work for a minute. "She played when we were kids," she said. "Christmas songs, badly, every December. I didn't know she still opened it."

"They usually do," Arthur said. "Quietly."

By late afternoon the light in the room had gone amber and the piano stood at pitch — A-440 through the middle, the treble stretched a breath sharp and the bass let a breath soft, the way pianos want it, the way ears expect it even when they don't know why. He tested octaves up and down the keyboard, struck chords and let them ring, and the room took the sound and held it — the empty room especially, which returns a piano's voice differently than a furnished one, more honestly, with nothing to absorb the overtones but wallpaper and time.

Then he sat down and played the eight bars. Just the opening of it, the way a nine-year-old would have learned it first, and the piano — persuaded, agreeing, sixty years of Margaret Ellison in its hammers — carried the phrase to the back wall and let it fade there.

"Is it worth anything?" Carol asked, when he'd packed up.

"It's in tune," Arthur said.

It was not an answer. It was the only one he had. He closed the door gently behind him, the way you do when a room is sleeping, and drove home through the blue end of the day with his hands quiet on the wheel, knowing — the way you know a last thing without deciding it — that somewhere behind him the piano was holding the pitch in the empty house, keeping the treaty, holding the note the whole world had agreed on, for whoever came next.

**Concert Pitch**

The call came on a Tuesday, the way most calls do — unremarkable, unhurried, a woman's voice asking if he still tuned pianos.

"I do," Arthur said.

"It was my mother's. She passed in March, and the house goes on the market next month. We don't know what to do with the piano. Could you look at it? Tell us honestly if it's worth saving."

He was seventy-nine. His hands had begun to file their own reports — a tremor in the mornings, a stiffness that took an hour to argue out of them. He had declared the last piano the last piano at least four times, and meant it each time.

"Saturday morning," he heard himself say. "I'll be there."

The house on Delmore Street was a two-story clapboard with the windows dark and the rooms going hollow around stacked boxes. The daughter — Carol, she said, shaking his hand like a business meeting — apologized for the mess. The piano stood against the front wall of the living room where the furniture used to be: a Baldwin upright, 1961 by the serial number, walnut veneer gone dull under a film of dust, but sound. Nobody had put a drink on it. Nobody had let the sun cook it. Somebody had loved it once, in the ordinary way people love things — by not quite neglecting them.

He raised the lid. The smell came up out of it: felt and old wood, a faint sweetness like a coat closet, dust with decades in it. He pressed the keys one at a time, ear tilted, and the piano told him its whole history in about ninety seconds. A quarter-tone flat overall — strings give up their tension by degrees across the years, the instrument sighing slowly down toward its resting pitch. The middle register worst. One dead note in the treble, a broken string. Two keys sticking. And underneath it all, a decent piano. Good bones, as the saying goes. His father had hated that saying. Pianos didn't have bones, he said. They had opinions, two hundred and thirty of them, one per string, and the tuner's job was to hold a meeting and get them to agree.

Arthur set out his tools on the bench: the tuning lever, the felt strip, the rubber wedges, the fork that hummed A-440 when you struck it — concert pitch, the note the whole world had agreed on, though nothing in physics required it. People had simply decided, together, what A should sound like. It was, his father liked to say, the only treaty that had never been broken.

He worked the way he'd worked for sixty years, which was slowly. Felt strip through the strings to silence the neighbors. Wedge in place. Lever on the pin, and then the listening — that slow wobble, the beat, when two tones are close enough to fight. You turn the pin a hair. A half-hair. The beat slows. Slows. Dies. On to the next. It was not, strictly speaking, work. It was attention, sustained for hours, and he had built a life out of it.

His hands, he noticed, were steady today.

The dead string he replaced from his case — the old one had rusted through at the bearing point. The sticking keys he freed, cleaned the felt, eased the bushings. And when he lifted the bench lid to make room, he found the music: lesson books, a hymnal, and on top a recital program gone soft at the folds. *Spring Recital, June 1954. Margaret Ellison, age 9 — Für Elise.* Penciled fingerings in the margins of the sheet music, in a child's careful hand, some of them wrong. He could see her: small, serious, the numbers copied out of a teacher's book, the same eight bars played four hundred times, because he could read it in the hammers too — the felt worn into grooves on exactly those notes, the left-hand figure and the melody above it, the grooves deepest where a child had practiced and a woman had returned to, off and on, for seventy years.

Carol brought him coffee around noon and watched him work for a minute. "She played when we were kids," she said. "Christmas songs, badly, every December. I didn't know she still opened it."

"They usually do," Arthur said. "Quietly."

By late afternoon the light in the room had gone amber and the piano stood at pitch — A-440 through the middle, the treble stretched a breath sharp and the bass let a breath soft, the way pianos want it, the way ears expect it even when they don't know why. He tested octaves up and down the keyboard, struck chords and let them ring, and the room took the sound and held it, the empty room especially, which returns a piano's voice differently than a furnished one, more honestly, with nothing to absorb the overtones but wallpaper and time.

Then he sat down and played the eight bars. Just the opening of it, the way a nine-year-old would have learned it first, and the piano — persuaded, agreeing, sixty years of Margaret Ellison in its hammers — carried the phrase to the back wall and let it fade there.

"Is it worth anything?" Carol asked, when he'd packed up.

"It's in tune," Arthur said.

It was not an answer. It was the only one he had. He closed the door gently behind him, the way you do when a room is sleeping, and drove home through the blue end of the day with his hands quiet on the wheel, knowing — the way you know a last thing without deciding it — that somewhere behind him the piano was holding the pitch in the empty house, keeping the treaty, holding the note the whole world had agreed on, for whoever came next.
